beats.say: While the city sleeps, Khalid ibn al-Walid orders a silent assault, exploiting the forgotten Roman aqueduct.
The Umayyad commander, Abu Ubaidah, watches from the citadel, unaware his own engineers had built that passage.
A sudden flood bursts, drowning the defending archers and opening the gate for the invaders.
The surprise entry shatters the myth that Damascus fell only after a prolonged siege.
Historical chronicles hide this tactic, but the 634 campaign diary of al-Waqidi records it plainly.
Within hours, the Rashidun banner flies over the Umayyad palace, a swift turnover unlike any other conquest.
The city's water supply, once a lifeline, becomes the attackers' secret weapon, turning defense into surrender.
By nightfall, Damascus yields, not from starvation, but from a cunning flood-engineered breach.
This hidden maneuver reshaped early Islamic expansion, proving that ingenuity, not numbers, won the city.
